title: Closed Timelike Curve Decoding on Quantum Hardware
abstract: Deutsch closed timelike curves (D-CTCs) are described by a fixed-point condition for a chronology-violating register. We study a finite-dimensional circuit model that places a Hayden--Preskill/Yoshida--Kitaev recovery map inside such a consistency loop. A register-routing construction makes the Deutsch map explicit: an initial SWAP moves the incoming CTC state to an idle dump register, the scrambler and decoder act on the remaining active registers, and a final SWAP writes the recovered message back to the CTC register. When the active branch recovers the message, the induced map on the CTC register is the replacement channel \(σ\mapsto ρ_M\), with the unique fixed point \(ρ_M\). We implement the associated Lloyd-type post-selected decoder circuits on quantum hardware and formulate a classical-feedback iteration for the experimentally estimated map. Qiskit simulations and IBM-hardware data for single-qubit instances quantify decoder fidelity, post-selection overhead, routing-dependent noise, and quantum-geometric susceptibility.
summary: This paper analyzes decoding information encoded within a theoretical Closed Timelike Curve framework on quantum hardware. It establishes the ideal fixed point for this process and then rigorously tests practical implementations by simulating and measuring fidelity using advanced error mitigation techniques. The work provides quantitative diagnostics on how noise affects the recovery of quantum information across complex, time-looping circuits.
main_problem: The study investigates how quantum information encoded via Closed Timelike Curves (CTCs) can be decoded on quantum hardware, particularly when considering noise effects.
main_result: The ideal circuit model predicts a unique fixed point for the CTC-input map ($\sigma^* = ho_M$), and hardware simulations confirm expected scaling overheads while quantifying noise impact via fidelity measurements.
method: The authors combine theoretical derivations of induced maps with practical quantum circuit implementations, utilizing post-selection, classical feedback iterations, and advanced error mitigation techniques like ZNE.
model_or_system: The model is a finite-dimensional quantum circuit implementing a Deutsch consistency loop containing a Hayden–Preskill/Yoshida–Kitaev recovery map. It involves multiple registers (CTC, Message, etc.) interacting via SWAPs and decoding operations.

important_parameters: Noise parameter $\delta$, message dimension $m$, and circuit parameters like rotation angles $(	heta, \phi)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on an ideal circuit model for theoretical proofs, while hardware sections approximate this using post-selection or classical feedback loops.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the CTC schematic, the register-separated Deutsch loop construction, and detailed diagnostics like Loschmidt echo probabilities ($P_{00}(\delta)$) comparing simulation to hardware fits.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical ideal fixed point ($\sigma^* = ho_M$) using circuit theory, through implementing approximate decoding methods (Lloyd-type/classical feedback), and finally characterizing performance on quantum hardware using echo measurements and fidelity analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on CTCs, the rigorous error characterization using Loschmidt echoes and the comparison of different resource scaling techniques (post-selection vs. dynamic feedforward) are highly relevant to understanding noise resilience in any complex quantum computation protocol.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of a closed timelike curve (CTC). A worldline traversing a wormhole-like geometry con- nects the present to its own past, forming a closed loop in spacetime. The figure motivates the finite-dimensional quantum-information models studied below.

FIG. 2. Register-separated ideal Deutsch-loop construction in the register order C, E, R, G, M, A, Y . The first SWAP transfers the prepared message ρM from M to C and routes the incoming CTC state σ to the dump wire Mdump, which remains a spectator thereafter. The scrambler Uscr acts on C, E, R, spreading the message information across these registers. The aligned blocks eDup and eDlow are the upper and lower graphical components of the same decoder dilation and together recover the message on Y . Algebraically, the active operation has the factorized form IMdump ⊗WC,E,R,G,A,Y . Every time we observe a bell pair on (R, G) or (E, M) or (A, Y), the decoder recovers ρM on Y , the final SWAP...

FIG. 3. Single-qubit, seven-qubit amplitude-amplified decoder circuit used in the hardware study. The first SWAP moves the prepared message ρM from M into C. In this hardware convention the would-be CTC input is initialized, so the post-SWAP wire labelled M is clean and can be reused inside the Bell-pair/conjugate-decoder block. The register-separated arbitrary-σ version is shown in Fig. 2.

FIG. 4. Probabilistic Yoshida–Kitaev decoder used as a Lloyd-type post-selected emulation for a multi-qubit message. The would-be CTC input is initialized in this compressed circuit, so the post-SWAP wires labelled M0, M1 can be used as auxiliary decoder wires. Runs are retained when the Bell measurements on (R0, G0) and (R1, G1) give the selected |Φ+⟩outcomes. The register-separated Deutsch replacement-channel circuit is the ideal construction in Fig. 2.

FIG. 5. Post-selection probability for the one- and two-qubit decoder-emulation circuits. The ideal values are psucc = 1/4 for m = 1 and psucc = 1/16 for m = 2. The hardware esti- mates are consistent with these Bell-projection probabilities within the displayed confidence intervals, confirming the ex- pected sampling overhead for the selected branch.
